title: Closing the Loop ep. 0012 — The law firm that's built a large and successful software business (David Wakeling, Allen & Overy)
pub: Closing the Loop (CTL Research) podcast, ep. 0012
author: Andrew Camel (host; David Wakeling is the guest)

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts technology-led redesign of legal delivery and materially extends the cluster with a concrete incumbent-firm example: software created to handle contract work at otherwise infeasible scale developed into a multidisciplinary operation managing dozens of products. It does not substantively address pricing, verification or the apprenticeship problem.
qs: 10 years later, Allen & Overy has dozens of different software products managed by an interdisciplinary team of lawyers, software engineers, and data scientists.

st.t: Harvey strategy: Prestige supports infrastructure ambitions
st.an: Wakeling accepts Harvey’s application-layer and governed-workflow logic, adding concrete adopter-side evidence of phased deployment, integration into drafting tools and broad reported use. He also materially develops the defensibility caveat by advocating vendor-portable design amid competition. His productivity claims remain estimates rather than independently validated findings, consistent with the cluster’s evidentiary limits.

st.an: Wakeling accepts that legal AI can support new products and meaningful firm-scale efficiency, and materially extends the cluster’s organisational-redesign proposition with two implementation principles: evaluate risk by use case and design products to remain portable across competing vendors. He does not establish that repeatable services or broader market transformation have already resulted.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Wakeling accepts the cluster’s bounded, human-in-the-loop view of legal AI and materially extends it with a use-case-specific risk standard: compare AI with the existing process and weigh errors by their consequences rather than requiring perfection. He also develops the institutional-absorption theme by locating value in products built between foundation models and lawyers, with vendor portability as a strategic design objective. His time-saving estimate supports production efficiency but is presented as organisational belief rather than independently measured evidence.

st.an: Wakeling aligns with the synthesis by treating legal-specific application-layer value and productivity gains as plausible but not conclusive evidence of defensibility. He materially extends it with a portability strategy: firms should anticipate vendor competition and design workflows so they can move between providers rather than depend on a durable Harvey moat.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Wakeling accepts the cluster’s core view that legal AI creates value through selective, risk-sensitive deployment and operating-model redesign rather than autonomous replacement. He materially extends it with a concrete productisation model: fixed-fee software for repetitive, templated work, lawyer handling of exceptions and quality control, plus comparative testing and vendor-portable system design.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: Wakeling supports the cluster’s view that legal AI strategy extends beyond tool acquisition to product and workflow design, while treating Harvey as one layer in a competitive value chain. His emphasis on use-case-specific risk, aggregate productivity and vendor-portable architecture also aligns with the synthesis’s cautions about verification, uncertain vendor durability and hybrid build-and-buy strategies.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Wakeling supports the cluster’s account of generative AI broadening addressable legal tasks and requiring workflow integration, phased governance, practitioner feedback and sustained iteration. His reported adoption figures reinforce the implementation theme, while remaining usage evidence rather than comparative proof of productivity, quality or durable specialist value.
qs: What use cases are most helpful?** **20:40  We tried to map out the functions of lawyers: "draft", "comment", "summarize", etc.

st.t: Workflow trust: Verification remains costly and contested
st.an: Wakeling directly supports the cluster’s core proposition that legal AI need not be error-free if risk is managed through use-case selection and workflow safeguards. He treats hallucination risk as irreducible but manageable through evidence-linked RAG, governance, contractual data protections and avoidance of high-risk applications; he does not establish that verification is costless or that autonomous reliance is safe.
qs: governance, evidence-based RAG (showing where answers come from), contractual agreements with 3rd-parties that ensure your data is being handled appropriately, staying away from risky areas, etc.

kp.k: Regulatory remediation drove legal software development
kp.d: Wakeling describes Margin Matrix as a response to post-Lehman regulatory work whose volume made manual delivery impractical. After selling to a major bank and remediating tens of thousands of contracts for that client, A&O partnered with Deloitte to scale delivery to more customers. This is an account of software-enabled legal delivery preceding its generative-AI adoption.
qs: The first project we did was Margin Matrix; introduced in response to work associated with new regulations post-Lehman

We built it, pitched it to some of the biggest banks around the world, and sold it successfully to one, and then were then delivering remediation on tens of thousands of contracts, for just one client
Chose to partner with Deloitte to "crank the machine" in many more customers
Start with business problem... there weren't going to be enough lawyers to handle this... it was just such a manual process

kp.d: The document describes the Markets Innovation Group as combining lawyers, developers and data scientists to change legal delivery through technology and alternative resource models. Wakeling reports dozens of products built on a common framework, including bond-document drafting, fund formation and loan execution tools; these are reported operational capabilities rather than predictions.
qs: David is a partner at the firm and leads the "Markets Innovation Group", which is made up of lawyers, developers, and data scientsts
Our job is to disrupt the existing legal model, turning to technology or resource models that enable us to do things differently
We now have dozens of small drawdown products off the core platform/framework

kp.k: Software licenses replace hourly pricing for standardized work
kp.d: For the initial product, Wakeling reports a fixed license fee tied to contract numbers at 1/3 the cost of manual lawyer work. Pricing incorporated anticipated quality-control costs. Most delivery was software-only, while the law firm could supply conventional legal resources for the reported 10% of exceptions the software could not handle.
qs: We came up with a fixed license fee per number of contracts, and it was 1/3 the cost of the alternative
We basically projected the work we thought we would need to do on quality control, to ensure we would be offsetting our internal costs as well
Most of the time it's just a software product, but being a law firm, we can provide a more conventional resource model for those 10% of "exceptions" that can't be handled by the software

kp.k: Successful products target repetition and regulatory dislocation
kp.d: Wakeling identifies heavily templated, repetitive, high-volume work and categories disrupted by events such as Brexit as the strongest product opportunities. His development account emphasizes client conversations around an MVP, using banks' structured data, integrating with customer workflows and limiting initial client numbers to avoid overwhelming delivery capacity.
qs: 1: Heavily templated, highly repetitive, high volume
2: Any categories subject to a dislocation event (e.g. Brexit)
I had to think about how it would be integrated into these banks' workflows
Once we had that plan done, we were away, but capped the number of clients to make sure we weren't overwhelmed

kp.k: Innovation requires experimentation and organizational patience
kp.d: Wakeling advises firms pursuing this model to accommodate an experimental group rather than expect immediate profitability. He stresses feedback loops and continuing iteration, presenting these as lessons from building the business.
qs: There's an organizational philosophy that needs to change; it's an experimental group, and it's going to take longer than 6 weeks to make money; the organization needs to understand that
You need to introduce feedback loops and constant iteration; having known this 5 years ago would have saved me a lot of time

kp.k: Generative AI deployment followed dedicated governance development
kp.d: Wakeling reports meeting Harvey in September before ChatGPT and obtaining GPT-4 beta access. Following sandbox testing, he allocated 10 team members to six weeks of safe-deployment governance work. A phased internal rollout targeted 2k lawyers by Christmas and generated 600 detailed survey responses, followed by integration into drafting tools.
qs: Last Sept we got to know Harvey, pre ChatGPT; through that we got access to GPT-4 in beta
I said "we're going to put everything into this"; I grabbed 10 people from my team and spend 6 weeks developing governance around safe deployment
Rolled out in phases with objective of 2k lawyers by X-Mas (all internal usage)
We got 600 very detailed responses to effectively an IT survey
Since then, we've been building this into our drafting tools

kp.k: Adoption and time savings are practitioner-reported
kp.d: At the interview, Wakeling reports 3.7k regular users of Harvey or Contract Matrix and average usage of 800 times a day, without clarifying the denominator for that usage figure. He separately estimates a couple of hours saved per week across 3.7k lawyers. The document supplies no measurement method or task-level savings breakdown.
qs: This morning, we had 3.7k people who are regular users of our genAI systems, either Harvey or Contract Matrix, and they use it on average 800 times a day
We believe we save a couple hours per week; across 3.7k lawyers, that's a lot of hours of lawyers' time

kp.k: Broad task applicability underpins transformation predictions
kp.d: Wakeling describes mapping lawyer functions such as drafting, commenting and summarizing, and claims the tools can affect almost every function when applied appropriately. He identifies bespoke provisions and translation as particularly effective current uses, while presenting data extraction and RAG, including transaction due diligence, as the next opportunity. His assertion of industry-wide transformation is a prediction rather than a demonstrated outcome.
qs: We tried to map out the functions of lawyers: "draft", "comment", "summarize", etc.
We discovered was that it's such a malleable tool, if you can point it at a use case in the right way, almost every function you can have an impact on
Coming up with bespoke provisions & translations of documents between languages -- it's incredibly effective
Dropping in datasets / data extraction / RAG is next one for us; that will really take off
That just affirmed the conclusion we'd reached, which is that this is going to completely transform the legal industry

kp.k: Safe deployment needs layered, use-specific safeguards
kp.d: Wakeling recommends governance, evidence-based RAG showing answer sources, third-party contractual protections for data and avoidance of risky uses. He says hallucination risk cannot be eliminated completely, while characterizing privacy and IP infringement as challenging but solvable and information security as requiring attention.
qs: It's a constellation of things you need to do right to allow this to work safely... governance, evidence-based RAG (showing where answers come from), contractual agreements with 3rd-parties that ensure your data is being handled appropriately, staying away from risky areas, etc.
Hallucination risk is not completely removable; you just need to build around this to the extent possible
Data privacy and IP infrigement -- those are also challenging, but solvable
Information security as well -- there are various sub-concerns & ways to solve for this, but it's important to think about

kp.k: Risk tolerance should reflect existing review limitations
kp.d: Wakeling argues that AI need not be perfect if it improves on existing practice. He contrasts companies' concern about reputational exposure with M&A due diligence where AI may cover data volumes that otherwise would not be reviewed. The 4% error risk appears in this discussion as an illustrative risk figure, not a reported measured hallucination rate.
qs: With hallucinations, it doesn't have to be perfect; it just needs to be better than the current position
A lot of what's happening right now is companies looking at it by accessing tabloid risk; "is this a use case where that 4% error risk will get me in page 4 of the tabloids?"
But there are other use cases where that 4% error risk isn't an issue; e.g. in M&A due diligence, where you wouldn't have been able to review that volume of data to begin with

kp.k: Competitive advantage lies in productized legal expertise
kp.d: Wakeling locates A&O's anticipated competitive advantage in governance, management of legal issues and practice precedents packaged into products, rather than exclusively in underlying AI technology. He frames product development around the space between foundation models, Harvey's legal adaptation and human users, while acknowledging uncertainty about competing for data-science talent.
qs: In terms of the value chain, we have a foundational model, we then have Harvey leveraging and tuning it for law, and then at the far other end you have a human using this product; what fits in between the human and the model?

People talk about moats being in the AI tech companies; we believe our moat is around governance, management of legal issues, practice precedents, etc.; our moat is in the productization of our expertise
The talent war on data science makes us nervous... for the things we build, we will be competing in this market... to what degree do we want to do this? can we hire the people we need?

kp.d: Wakeling advocates designs that can move between vendors, warning that dependence on particular providers may leave businesses exposed. He reports an operational toggle between model providers with feedback on performance and stresses testing to establish that switching remains possible. He qualifies current portability by predicting greater difficulty over time.
qs: Our objective is to future-proof our design so we can port everything between vendors as needed
A lot of businesses could get lulled into dependencies on specific providers; that may put them in a very tough position
Effective testing then becomes very important as well; you need to know you can switch if needed
We have a toggle; we can flip between model providers and allow a mini feedback loop to see how each model is performing
The way we're using it, not as much as you'd think, but it will get trickier over time

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: David Wakeling claims generative AI can improve almost every legal function and will transform the legal industry.
pts.d: Wakeling attributes this conclusion to A&O's experience mapping lawyers' functions, including drafting, commenting and summarising, against the capabilities of its generative-AI tools. He identifies bespoke provisions and translation as particularly effective current applications. This is a broad practitioner claim and prediction, not a reported comparative test of every legal function.

pts.k: Wakeling estimates that A&O's generative-AI tools save lawyers a couple of hours each week.
pts.d: He describes time savings across approximately 3,700 lawyers and reports substantial internal adoption of Harvey and Contract Matrix. The framing is augmentation of lawyers using the products, not replacement of lawyers or unsupervised delivery of legal advice. The source does not establish whether saved hours translate into lower client prices, higher profits or reduced staffing.

pts.k: Wakeling predicts growth in AI-assisted extraction and retrieval over datasets, including transaction due diligence.
pts.d: He identifies dataset ingestion, data extraction and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) as the next area of development. He also argues that AI can enable review of volumes of M&A material that would otherwise go unreviewed. This presents AI as expanding practical review capacity, rather than merely accelerating an unchanged manual process.

pts.k: Wakeling argues that useful legal AI does not require eliminating hallucinations, but does require governance and use-case-specific risk management.
pts.d: He claims hallucination risk cannot be completely removed and should instead be managed around the application. He presents data privacy and intellectual-property infringement as challenging but solvable, and identifies information security as another concern. His proposed safeguards include showing the sources behind answers, appropriate third-party contractual arrangements and avoiding risky applications. His comparison is with the current position, including work that could not otherwise be undertaken, rather than an ideal of error-free output. The discussion of a 4% error risk is illustrative; the document does not identify it as a measured error rate for Harvey, Contract Matrix or a specific model.

pts.k: Wakeling argues that law firms can capture AI-related value by turning their expertise and governance capabilities into products.
pts.d: He locates A&O's potential competitive advantage in governance, management of legal issues and practice precedents, rather than solely in the underlying AI technology. In his account, foundation models and Harvey's legal adaptation sit upstream of products used by humans, leaving opportunities to build around them. He also identifies competition for data-science talent as a constraint on how much a law firm can build itself. These are strategic assessments rather than measured findings about market-wide value distribution.

pts.k: Wakeling predicts that dependence on particular AI providers can become a business risk and advocates portable product design.
pts.d: He says A&O seeks to move its products between vendors as needed and already uses a toggle and feedback loop to compare model performance. He reports that switching requires less product change than might be expected for its current applications, while anticipating greater difficulty over time. Testing model performance here is distinct from human verification of individual legal outputs.

pts.k: As context for the AI strategy, Wakeling claims legal software can scale contract work and replace much manual delivery with fixed-fee products.
pts.d: His earlier Margin Matrix and document-automation experience concerns legal software, not necessarily generative AI. He reports that post-financial-crisis contract remediation exceeded practical lawyer capacity, that the software was priced at one-third of the manual alternative through a licence fee tied to contract volume, and that conventional lawyer services remained available for approximately 10% of exceptions. He identifies repetitive, templated, high-volume work and regulatory or market dislocations as especially successful product opportunities. These earlier software results should not be treated as measured cost reductions from LLMs.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is principally Wakeling's first-hand account of A&O's deployment, internal feedback and product-building experience.
pts.d: Wakeling speaks as a partner, head of the Markets Innovation Group and leader of the firm's global AI strategy. He describes sandbox testing of GPT-4 through Harvey, six weeks of governance development with ten team members, phased internal deployment and 600 detailed survey responses. He reports approximately 3,700 regular generative-AI users and average use of 800 times a day, but the supplied wording does not unambiguously specify the denominator for that usage figure. His weekly time-saving estimate has no stated measurement method or task-level breakdown. Earlier software evidence includes tens of thousands of contracts for one client, a Deloitte partnership to expand delivery and dozens of products. No independent benchmark, controlled productivity study, measured hallucination rate or financial results for the generative-AI products are supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source distinguishes current deployment experience in the 2023 interview from undated forecasts of industry transformation and further product development.
pts.d: Current claims include internal use, estimated weekly savings, effective drafting and translation, and model-switching capabilities. Adoption is described through relative dates: contact with Harvey 'Last Sept', a pre-ChatGPT introduction, and a rollout target of 2,000 lawyers by Christmas. The supplied document does not give a precise interview date from which to resolve every relative reference. Data extraction and RAG are described as next steps; complete industry transformation and more difficult model switching have no specified deadline. Claimed benefits depend on directing the tool appropriately, implementing safeguards and selecting suitable risks. Building a software business also requires an organisation willing to fund experimentation beyond a short-term return horizon and support repeated iteration.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The concrete examples primarily concern a large business-law firm, its lawyers and technical teams, and major institutional clients.
pts.d: A&O lawyers are described as gaining time and support across legal functions. Banks and transactional clients receive scalable contract remediation, automated documentation and potentially broader due-diligence coverage. The firm can sell software licences while supplying conventional legal resources for exceptions. Its interdisciplinary team of lawyers, developers and data scientists builds and maintains these products, with technical recruitment becoming a strategic concern. Harvey and foundation-model providers supply upstream technology; Deloitte is described as a delivery-scaling partner in the earlier Margin Matrix business. Although Wakeling predicts transformation of the legal industry generally, the supplied examples do not establish specific effects on small firms, entry-level employment, consumer legal services or access to justice.
